beats.script_body: A number of gay-owned businesses once lined MacDougal St, among them the legendary Eve's Hangout at number 129, a tearoom run by Polish Jewish immigrant Eva Kotchever, known as Eve Addams. Police raided the place in June 1926, charging Eve with 'obscenity' for penning her Lesbian Love anthology and deporting her to Europe. There she ran a bookstore and club in Paris, fought in the Spanish Civil War, and was eventually imprisoned and murdered in Auschwitz. Playwright Barbara Kahn wrote Unreachable Eden about Kotchever's life.

beats.script_body: By the 1890s, the rough-and-ready Lower East Side had a reputation for scandalous 'resorts' — dancing halls, saloons and brothels frequented by the city's 'inverts' and 'fairies.' From Paresis Hall at 5th St and Bowery to Slide at 157 Bleecker St, these venues offered cross-dressing spectaculars, dancing, and back rooms for same-sex encounters. beats.source_passage: By the 1890s, New York City's rough-and-ready Lower East Side had established quite a reputation for scandalous 'resorts' – dancing halls, saloons and brothels – frequented by the city's 'inverts' and 'fairies.' From Paresis Hall at 5th St and Bowery to Slide at 157 Bleecker St, these venues offered everything from cross-dressing spectaculars and dancing to back rooms for same-sex encounters. For closeted middle-class men, these dens were a secret thrill – places reached undercover on trains for a fix of camaraderie, understanding and uninhibited fun. For curious middle-class straights, they were just as enticing – salacious destinations on voyeuristic 'slumming tours.'

beats.script_body: Harlem's drag balls became a hit with gay and straight New Yorkers in the roaring '20s. The biggest was the Hamilton Lodge Ball, run by Lodge #710 of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows and held annually at the swank Rockland Palace on 155th St. Commonly dubbed the Faggots Ball, it let men and women legally cross-dress and steal a same-sex dance, with a beauty pageant crowning the 'Queen of the Ball.' Langston Hughes called it the 'spectacles of color,' and the gay writer was one of many literati to attend; the papers covered the outrageous frocks as the talk of the town.

It crowned a 'Queen of the Ball'; Langston Hughes called it 'spectacles of color' and attended
beats.source_passage: Even more famous were Harlem's drag balls, which became a hit with both gay and straight New Yorkers in the roaring '20s. The biggest of the lot was the Hamilton Lodge Ball, organized by Lodge #710 of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows and held annually at the swank Rockland Palace on 155th St. Commonly dubbed the Faggots Ball, it was a chance for both gay men and women to (legally) cross-dress and steal a same-sex dance, and for fashionable 'normals' to indulge in a little voyeuristic titillation. The evening's star attraction was the beauty pageant, which saw the drag-clad competitors vie for the title of 'Queen of the Ball.' Langston Hughes proclaimed it the 'spectacles of color' and the gay writer was one of many members of New York's literati to attend the ball.

beats.script_body: LGBTIQ+ activism intensified as AIDS hit headlines in the early 1980s. Writer Larry Kramer helped found ACT UP — the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power — in 1987 to fight perceived homophobia and the price-gouging of AIDS drugs. One of its boldest protests came on September 14, 1989, when seven ACT UP protesters chained themselves to the VIP balcony of the New York Stock Exchange, demanding that Burroughs Wellcome lower the price of the AIDS drug AZT from a prohibitive $10,000 per patient per year. Within days, the price was slashed to $6400.

beats.source_passage: Out of his efforts was born ACT UP (AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power) in 1987, an advocacy group set up to fight the perceived homophobia and indifference of then-president Ronald Reagan, as well as to end the price gouging of AIDS drugs by pharmaceutical companies. One of its boldest protests took place on September 14, 1989, when seven ACT UP protesters chained themselves to the VIP balcony of the New York Stock Exchange, demanding pharmaceutical company Burroughs Wellcome lower the price of AIDS drug AZT from a prohibitive $10,000 per patient per annum. Within days, the price was slashed to $6400 per patient.

name: Stonewall Inn
short_description: Birthplace of the modern LGBTQ rights movement (1969 riots); a US National Monument. Very high gravity.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Birthplace of the modern LGBTQ rights movement (1969 riots); a US National Monument. Very high gravity.

gravity_audit.reasoning: Wikipedia article is extensive covering the 1969 riots and LGBTQ history in detail. Part of Stonewall National Monument. No official annual visitor count found; very high cultural prominence globally.

beats.script_body: By the 1940s and '50s, the relative transgression of the early 20th century had given way to a new conservatism — the Great Depression, WWII and the Cold War took their toll, and Senator Joseph McCarthy declared that homosexuals in the State Department threatened America's security and children. Tougher policing forced the queer scene underground, and crackdowns on gay venues grew increasingly common. Yet on June 28, 1969, when police raided the Stonewall Inn — a gay-friendly watering hole in Greenwich Village — patrons did the unthinkable: they revolted. Fed up with harassment and with corrupt officers taking payoffs from the bars' mostly organized-crime owners, they bombarded the police with coins, bottles, bricks and chants of 'gay power' and 'we shall overcome.' They were met by a line of high-kicking drag queens and their now-legendary chant. The collective anger and solidarity was a turning point, igniting passionate debate about discrimination and forming the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement — not just in New York but across the US and in countries from the Netherlands to Australia. On the one-year anniversary, the day was marked by the US's first LGBTIQ+ Pride march.

physical_cues.cue: The Stonewall Inn storefront on Christopher Street, site of the June 1969 raid

key_claims: 1940s-50s conservatism, McCarthy targeted homosexuals, policing forced the scene underground
On June 28, 1969 police raided the Stonewall Inn and patrons revolted, throwing coins, bottles, bricks
Riot was the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement; first Pride march held on the one-year anniversary
beats.source_passage: The relative transgression of the early 20th century was replaced with a new conservatism in the following decades, as the Great Depression, WWII and the Cold War took their toll. Conservatism was helped along by Senator Joseph 'Joe' McCarthy, who declared that homosexuals in the State Department threatened America's security and children. Tougher policing aimed to eradicate queer visibility in the public sphere, forcing the scene further underground in the 1940s and '50s. Yet on June 28, 1969, when police officers raided the Stonewall Inn – a gay-friendly watering hole in Greenwich Village – patrons did the unthinkable: they revolted. Fed up with both the harassment and corrupt officers receiving payoffs from the bars' owners (who were mostly organized-crime figures), they began bombarding the officers with coins, bottles, bricks and chants of 'gay power' and 'we shall overcome.' Their collective anger and solidarity was a turning point, igniting intense and passionate debate about discrimination and forming the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement, not just in New York, but across the US and in countries from the Netherlands to Australia. On the one-year anniversary of the riots, the day was marked by the US's first LGBTIQ+ Pride march.
